Spent some time this afternoon carrying back learnings about intercepting API requests from the ArkPes implementation back to Dynamo this afternoon, and my initial spike is very promising. Every variant of the dynamo data rooms I've seen share the same base set of APIs with the same structure, and there's a configurable columns parameter that allows us to request the upload date, even if the data room frontend doesn't request/display it. I had previously refined a really complicated set of instructions for claude for how to decide which date column to use depending on how the frontend rendered table, and I think we can get rid of all of that by following the same ArkPes pattern - 1. Log in, set auth cookie in browser 2. Click into a data room 3. Capture network requests, pull out relevant parameters that load docs 4. Reform and refetch network requests with desired columns + filters 5. Download directly from API response The dynamo reference guide was reasonably well followed, but the portals are genuinely hard to navigate - sometimes you have to reset filters, scroll horizontally across the entire table, click a column header, etc. just to see what you can filter on and sort on. This approach circumvents all of that. The notable risk/con of this approach is that it ties us more concretely to the dynamo APIs. I'm not concerned about their APIs changing quickly, so I still think this is a better approach, but wanted to call it out for awareness. cc

I still think this the better approach, but it's less the vision of 'just tell claude how you'd use the website'. Got a good bulk feedback loop running locally now and was able to refine the subagent-driven approach further with this strategy. I merged in two new updates to the plugin yesterday that should notably improve consistency and instruction-following in all the subagents that perform login, document discovery, etc. How it works: 1. I ran 12 parallel runs for a single portal at the same time, and then package up the `.jsonl` logs from the main session and all the subagents in the exact same way the CLI telemetry commands do 2. For all 12 session logs, I ran the new `portal-session-analyze` skill I added to the plugin that reads the logs, compares against the instructions, and finds opportunities to improve instruction adherence, wasted tool calls, inefficiencies, etc. 3. Based on these findings, I built a plan to address these issues 4. Then, I did a follow up run with another 12 parallel sessions and re-ran the same analysis process to confirm the issues were addressed Resulting PR here: < Portal automation subagent prompt efficiency improvements>

My first run of this approach also surfaced an interesting finding The first subagent-driven approach I took just told the main session "Assemble a prompt yourself with all of these references and pass it to a subagent" For the first subagents, it generated full, comprehensive prompts, but there was a strong degradation over time - e.g. the first subprompt was 12k characters for one portal, and the last ones lost half of that content. The subagents were generally good enough to pick up the missing pieces, but this loss of context caused a lot of extra work to figure out how to accomplish the task, since so much of the useful details were missed. With this feedback loop, I implemented a new version that builds the subprompts deterministically with a script packaged alongside - the initial results have been much stronger - all the subagents have much much more consistent performance from the beginning of the run to the end.
